newsitem.title: USA: US futures regulator calls for global cooperation.
newsitem.headline: US futures regulator calls for global cooperation.

text.p: Improved international cooperation among derivatives regulators is needed to police the increasingly global marketplace, a top U.S. regulator said.

"Just as capital knows no borders in today's financial marketplace, neither does fraud," Joseph Dial, commissioner at the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, said in a prepared speech released here. "If regulators are to have any hope of keeping pace with these developments, they must cooperate with each other and with industry self-regulatory bodies."

Dial, who was scheduled to speak Friday at the University of London's Institute of Advanced Legal Studies, said the need for such cooperation was clearly demonstrated in recent market scandals surrounding Barings Bank and Sumitomo Corp.
Dial also endorsed the conclusions of a report released in September that grew out of a meeting of international regulators in May 1995.

"The final report of (that meeting), released just last month, lists an impressive array of concrete steps," Dial said. "Taken together, these steps should minimize the systemic effects of any future market disruptions."

Sumitomo's shocking announcement in June that it had lost $1.8 billion in allegedly unauthorized copper trading provided the "first concrete test" of global information sharing agreements implemented by regulators in the wake of the Barings scandal, Dial said. Sumitomo later raised its loss estimate to $2.6 billion.
The agreements worked but "they could have worked better," he said, alluding to delays the CFTC faced in obtaining information about Sumitomo's positions from U.K. regulators.
Speaking hypothetically, Dial said delays occur when a regulator requests a broad array of information from its counterpart in another jurisdiction.
"B may not fully appreciate why A is asking for all this data and just what A plans to do with it," Dial said. "While questions are being resolved, the information exchange is delayed."

Dial said the CFTC's investigation of Sumitomo is ongoing and "likely to drag on for many months." The commission is looking for violations of the Commodity Exchange Act through market manipulation or other misconduct, he said.
He also predicted that some form of commodity law reform would pass the U.S. Congress next year, but added, "it will be different, perhaps very different, from the versions first introduced."

Earlier this year, Senators Richard Lugar, an Indiana Republican, and Patrick Leahy, a Vermont Democrat, introduced a bill to amend the Commodity Exchange Act, as did Congressman Thomas Ewing, an Illinois Republican. Both bills died when Congress wrapped up the legislative session. Both are expected to be reintroduced, possibly with changes, next year.
The bills would give the CFTC additional responsibility or authority for foreign futures contracts that are deliverable in the United States.
